title: The Production Code
objective: After this level you can explain why Hollywood censored itself under the Production Code from 1934 and why a ratings system replaced it in 1968.
summary: To head off government censorship, Hollywood adopted the Production Code in 1930 and enforced it from 1934. Television, foreign films and a 1952 ruling weakened it; ratings replaced it in 1968.

cards.headline: From 1934 to 1968, Hollywood's own rulebook decided what you could see.
cards.body: No government office wrote it. The studios did, and they enforced it on themselves. Why would an industry that sold thrills sign up to cut them?

cards.headline: Censor yourself, or be censored
cards.body: In 1922 studio heads formed a trade group, the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, and hired Will H. Hays to lead it. In 1930 it adopted the Production Code, drafted by Catholic publisher Martin Quigley and Jesuit priest Daniel Lord. The reason was self-defense: the code answered public outcry and the threat of government censorship. Better a rulebook you write than one written for you.

cards.headline: 1934: the code gets teeth
cards.body: The code needed enforcement. In 1934, as the Catholic Legion of Decency called for boycotts of films it found offensive, Hays set up the Production Code Administration under Joseph Breen. Members agreed to distribute only films it approved. The code forbade profanity, obscenity and graphic violence and crime, and insisted that good and evil never be confused.

cards.headline: Why it faded
cards.body: After World War II, television and foreign films, both outside the code's reach, undermined it. Then in 1952, in Burstyn v. Wilson, the Supreme Court ruled that films communicate ideas and couldn't face government censorship. The threat that made the code worth keeping was gone. In 1968 the code was replaced by the age-based rating system still used today.

title: Technicolor
objective: After this level you can explain how three-strip Technicolor recorded color and why black and white stayed common into the 1960s.
summary: Three-strip Technicolor split light into three black-and-white records and printed them in dye. Costly rented cameras kept most films black and white until the 1960s.

cards.headline: The famous color camera held only black-and-white film.
cards.body: Three-strip Technicolor cameras recorded nothing but black-and-white images. Yet the prints came out in full color. How did that work, and why did so many films stay black and white for decades afterward?

cards.headline: One lens, three films
cards.body: Behind the lens sat a beam-splitting cube. It divided the incoming light three ways, one beam favoring red, one green and one blue, and each beam exposed its own strip of black-and-white film. Each strip was a record of one color. The process was perfected in 1932 and introduced in Disney's cartoon Flowers and Trees, then in the feature Becky Sharp in 1935.

cards.headline: Putting the color back
cards.body: The color went in at the lab. The three strips were developed and printed separately, each print passed through its matching dye, and the three were laid together into one print. Stack the red, green and blue records and you get a reasonably faithful copy of natural color, a bit like three stencils printing one poster.

cards.headline: Why gray lasted
cards.body: Color was hard to get. Studios couldn't buy the heavy, costly cameras; Technicolor rented them out, with a color consultant from a team headed by Natalie Kalmus. In the early 1950s single-strip Eastmancolor negatives took over, and the three-strip camera was retired. Even so, color was less revolutionary than sound: silent film vanished quickly, but most features have been in color only since the 1960s.

title: Citizen Kane
objective: After this level you can explain why Citizen Kane's deep focus, low angles and jumbled timeline made it a film that filmmakers study.
summary: Citizen Kane (1941) used Gregg Toland's deep focus, low angles under muslin ceilings, and flashbacks from five witnesses; a box-office disappointment, it became one of the most influential films.

cards.headline: A 1941 box-office disappointment became the film filmmakers study.
cards.body: Orson Welles made Citizen Kane at RKO when he was 25, directing, co-writing it with Herman Mankiewicz and playing the lead. Critics praised it, ticket sales disappointed, and it won a single Oscar, for its screenplay. Three choices turned it into a textbook: what's sharp, where the camera sits and when things happen.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the lens recipe. Remember the result: near and far, all sharp, and you pick where to look.

cards.headline: Everything in focus
cards.body: Cinematographer Gregg Toland wanted the whole frame sharp, near and far. With faster Eastman film, wide-angle lenses set to small openings and powerful arc lamps, he reached a depth of field close to your own eye's. In nearly every scene, faces and objects are sharp in all parts of the screen, so the film lets you choose where to look.

cards.headline: Looking up at Kane
cards.body: Welles and Toland often set the camera low and shot upward. That meant trouble: Hollywood sets usually had no ceilings, because the lights hung from the rafters. So Toland had ceilings made of muslin cloth, which also let microphones hide just above them. In 1941, those low-angled shots that revealed ceilings looked powerful and modern.

cards.headline: A life in pieces
cards.body: The film opens with Kane's death. A reporter then questions people who knew him, and the story unfolds in flashbacks: the shifting, not always reliable accounts of five former intimates. Welles called it prismatic. You assemble Kane yourself, like a detective with clashing witnesses. It's one reason Citizen Kane became one of the most influential films ever made.

title: The Hollywood Blacklist
objective: After this level you can explain why the Hollywood blacklist began in 1947, how blacklisted writers kept working in secret, and how it ended.
summary: In 1947 HUAC investigated communism in Hollywood. The Hollywood Ten refused to answer, citing the First Amendment, and went to prison; a blacklist followed until Trumbo's 1960 credits.

cards.headline: In 1956 an Oscar went to a screenwriter who didn't exist.
cards.body: The Brave One's credited writer, Robert Rich, was a false name. The real author was Dalton Trumbo, who couldn't work in Hollywood under his own. How did an industry end up with some of its best writers working in secret?

cards.headline: The committee comes to Hollywood
cards.body: In 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee, set up in 1938, turned to the movies. It held that the American communist movement was foreign-controlled and a threat to national security, and it asked whether communist propaganda was getting into films. More than 100 witnesses were called about their own and their associates' alleged communist ties.

cards.headline: Ten who refused
cards.body: Ten of them, eight screenwriters and two directors, refused to answer questions about communist affiliations. They argued that the First Amendment protected their beliefs and associations from government inquiry. They were convicted of contempt of Congress and sentenced to six months to a year in prison. Studio heads fired them, and an unofficial blacklist followed: no work for anyone even suspected of communist ties.

cards.headline: Writing in the shadows
cards.body: Most of the Ten never worked in Hollywood again, but some wrote under false names. The blacklist cracked in 1960, when Trumbo received screen credit for Exodus and Spartacus, and it had disappeared by the early 1960s. The committee, long criticized for violating First Amendment rights, lost influence in the 1960s and was dissolved in 1975.

summary: As TV kept people home, attendance fell by almost half from 1946 to 1956. Hollywood went wide: three-projector Cinerama in 1952, then CinemaScope's squeezed image in 1953.

cards.headline: Movies in the home

cards.headline: CinemaScope: squeeze and stretch

title: What a Genre Promises
objective: After this level you can explain why a genre works as a promise between filmmakers and audiences about what they will feel.
summary: A genre promises something familiar and something new. Long familiarity trains viewers' expectations, and studios liked genres because reused sets and steady teams made filmmaking quicker.

cards.headline: You know how a Western goes before the lights go down.
cards.body: Cowboys, a dusty town, a showdown. You haven't seen a single frame, and you already have a list. Most genres are named by their subject or setting: the Western, the gangster film, the police thriller, science fiction. The name on the poster is a kind of promise. What exactly does it promise?

mascot.line: Keep this: a genre promises the familiar and the new at once. Every level in this chapter is that promise, one genre at a time.

cards.headline: Same again, but different
cards.body: Britannica puts the genre deal neatly: a genre promises a waiting audience something similar to what it has enjoyed before, and yet something quite new and different. That's the tightrope. All sameness and the film is a rerun. All newness and it breaks the promise you bought a ticket for. Think of your favorite pizza place trying one new topping, not turning into a sushi bar.

cards.headline: You walk in already trained
cards.body: Viewers knew, to a great extent, what to expect from a genre film. They recognized its stars, or at least its characters, and years of watching had made them sensitive to its music, its lighting and its plot devices. A chord in the score or a shadow on a wall could tell them what was coming. Every film you watch in a genre quietly trains you for the next one.

cards.headline: Why studios loved a formula
cards.body: Genres also suited a factory. A studio that planned half a dozen police thrillers in one year could reuse sets, costumes and props, saving time and money. Better still, it could keep the same writers, directors, crews and actors on the same genre, so they built a routine. That routine often made filmmaking quicker and better from one film to the next. The promise to audiences doubled as a production plan.

title: The Western
objective: After this level you can explain why the Western became America's defining genre and how its picture of Native Americans changed over time.
summary: The Western, basically an American creation, set its pattern in 1903, was revived by Stagecoach in 1939 and filled TV in the late 1950s. Later Westerns shifted sympathy toward Native Americans.

cards.headline: One genre grew out of America's own past.
cards.body: The Western is set in the American West, usually from the 1850s to the end of the 19th century. Britannica calls it basically an American creation, and the Library of Congress calls it a historically inspired genre invented in the United States. How did one country's frontier become a whole genre?

cards.headline: A pattern set in 1903
cards.body: You've met the Western's first big hit already. Britannica dates the Western film from The Great Train Robbery (1903), which set the pattern for many films that followed. The pattern came with a cast list: cowboys, a town sheriff, a U.S. marshal. And its conflicts tend to be settled the hard way, with violence and physical courage. The formula could fit on a wanted poster.

cards.headline: From B movie to prime time
cards.body: By the late 1930s the Western had long been stuck as a cheap B movie. Then John Ford's Stagecoach (1939), starring John Wayne, was a critical and commercial success that revitalized the genre. Westerns rode onto television too: series such as Gunsmoke and Bonanza drew large audiences in the late 1950s and the 1960s. The frontier was on the big screen and in the living room.

cards.headline: Who the Western got wrong
cards.body: One of the Western's basic themes is conflict between white pioneers and Native Americans. For decades, Britannica notes, films showed Native Americans with remarkably little understanding or appreciation. Later Westerns shifted sympathy toward them, among them John Ford's own Cheyenne Autumn (1964), Little Big Man (1970) and Dances with Wolves (1990). The genre that had told one side of the frontier began to tell the other.

title: The Musical
objective: After this level you can explain how musicals use song and dance to show feelings too big for speech.
summary: Busby Berkeley filmed dancers from overhead inside thin stories; Astaire filmed couples in full figure as statements of love. Later musicals, like Singin' in the Rain, let song carry the big moments.

cards.headline: People burst into song. Why doesn't it feel silly?
cards.body: In real life, nobody sings when they fall in love. In a musical, it's the main event. Britannica defines a musical film as a motion picture whose plot integrates musical numbers. The key word is integrates, and Hollywood took a while to work out how.

cards.headline: Busby Berkeley puts the camera on the ceiling
cards.body: In the early 1930s, Busby Berkeley staged elaborate dance sequences inside well-worn stories, in films such as 42nd Street (1933). His signature move: he placed the camera directly above the action, so rows of performers moved in precise geometric formations, like a kaleidoscope. No seat in a theater gives you that view. The story was mostly a frame for the spectacle.

cards.headline: Fred Astaire keeps it simple
cards.body: By the mid-1930s, singing and dancing teams had overtaken Berkeley's spectacles in popularity, above all Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, as in Top Hat (1935). Astaire simplified the musical: dancers were shot in full figure, with a minimum of edits and camera angles. Their routines at RKO worked as sophisticated statements of romantic love. The dance wasn't a break from the story. It was the courtship.

cards.headline: When a feeling is too big for talk
cards.body: Musicals of the late 1930s and 1940s, such as The Wizard of Oz (1939), moved toward greater unification of plot and music. In Singin' in the Rain (1952), song and dance, not dialogue, carry the important moments. Gene Kelly's character doesn't explain that he's in love: he swings from a lamppost in a downpour, singing. A speech would describe the feeling. The number lets you feel it.

title: Screwball Comedy
objective: After this level you can explain why fast-talking screwball comedies of the 1930s pitted sharp-witted couples against each other.
summary: Screwball comedies paired mismatched lovers who fought in fast, overlapping dialogue. Depression audiences wanted people beating adversity, and the Hays Code swapped sex for sparring.

cards.headline: In 1934, a comedy about a runaway heiress swept the Oscars.
cards.body: Frank Capra's It Happened One Night follows a runaway heiress and the reporter who tracks her down. It became the first film to win all five major Academy Awards, and it helped set the rules for a new kind of comedy: the screwball. Why would a love story work best as a fight?

cards.headline: Mismatched, and made for each other
cards.body: Screwball comedies put seemingly mismatched lovers at the center of unlikely romances, surrounded by off-the-wall characters and zany situations. In Bringing Up Baby (1938), Katharine Hepburn's eccentric heiress pursues Cary Grant's bookish paleontologist through one farcical mishap after another. The couples are often elegantly dressed in Art Deco rooms, and their shared talent for mischief is the proof they belong together.

cards.headline: Talk fast, and talk over each other
cards.body: Director Howard Hawks made overlapping dialogue one of his trademarks, and His Girl Friday (1940) is famous for its rapid-fire delivery. Hawks took The Front Page, a story about a newspaper editor and his reporter, and changed the pair from two men to a man and a woman: Cary Grant and Rosalind Russell. Now every argument about the job was also an argument about the two of them.

cards.headline: Why all the arguing?
cards.body: During the Depression, with film attendance in decline, studios wanted stories that showed people triumphing over adversity. They also had a rulebook. The Hays Code, Hollywood's own guidelines from 1934 to 1968, banned explicit mention of sexual relationships. So, as Britannica puts it, verbal sparring and physical comedy took the place of sexuality. In a screwball comedy, the quarrel is the love scene.

title: Horror
objective: After this level you can explain why audiences choose to be scared and how horror films build dread before the shock.
summary: A 2020 haunted-house study found enjoyment peaks at a just-right amount of fear. Cat People (1942) never shows its monster, letting shadows, silence and imagination build dread.

cards.headline: Why would anyone pay to be frightened?
cards.body: Britannica defines a horror film as one calculated to cause intense repugnance, fear or dread. That sounds like a product nobody would buy. Yet people line up for it. So researchers went into a haunted house to find out why.

cards.headline: A haunted house full of heart monitors
cards.body: In a 2020 study, researchers fitted 110 visitors to a commercial haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, with heart rate monitors, then asked how scared they felt and how much they enjoyed it. They were studying recreational fear: feeling fear and enjoyment at the same time. It sounds like a contradiction. Anyone who has laughed right after a scream knows it isn't.

cards.headline: Scared, but just right
cards.body: The results traced an upside-down U. Visitors who were barely scared enjoyed the house less, and so did those who were too scared. Enjoyment peaked at a just-right amount of fear. The researchers compare it to play: the fun comes from just-right departures from your body's normal state. Think of a horror film as a dial, and the filmmakers trying to leave it in the sweet spot.

mascot.line: Keep this: dread is the waiting, and it's built from what you can't quite see. Level 58 shows why knowing more makes waiting worse.

cards.headline: The cat you never see
cards.body: Horror doesn't have to show its monster. Cat People (1942), produced by Val Lewton for RKO on a skeletal budget, never shows its heroine Irena in cat form. It relies on suggestion and your imagination: shadows and low lighting build the suspense, and silences are held long enough to turn into dread. Your imagination draws a scarier cat than any costume could.

title: Film Noir
objective: After this level you can explain why film noir's shadowy crime stories flourished in the 1940s and what gave them their dark look.
summary: French critics named film noir after the war. Its high-contrast lighting isolates the hero, its stories came from hard-boiled novels, and its gloom matched postwar disillusion.

cards.headline: America's darkest crime films got their name in French.
cards.body: During the war, American films were banned in occupied countries. From 1946 they became available across Europe, and French critics admired a batch of Hollywood crime films for their cold, cynical characters and dark, brooding style. They called them film noir: dark film.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the list of titles. Remember the look: hard shadows that leave one person alone in the frame.

cards.headline: Shadows that leave the hero alone
cards.body: Noir's most notable visual feature is stark, high-contrast lighting: hard light, deep black shadow. It isn't only moody. It underscores how cut off the noir hero is from everyone else. Add rain-soaked streets and flashing neon signs. The look traces back to German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920). Light the scene evenly, and the loneliness drains away.

cards.headline: Stories from hard-boiled novels
cards.body: Noir took many of its stories from tough crime fiction. The Maltese Falcon (1941), John Huston's first film as director, adapted Dashiell Hammett's hard-boiled detective novel of 1930, and some consider it the first major work of noir. Double Indemnity (1944), directed by Billy Wilder, came from a novel by James M. Cain, with Raymond Chandler as co-writer. The cynics arrived already written.

cards.headline: Why the 1940s?
cards.body: Britannica ties noir's gloom to postwar disillusionment: an unstable peacetime economy, McCarthyism and the looming threat of atomic warfare. Its makers mattered too. European-born directors such as Billy Wilder and Fritz Lang, trained to stress style, often felt like outsiders in the Hollywood studio system, and noir drew them in. Outsiders made films about outsiders.

title: Science Fiction
objective: After this level you can explain why science fiction films use imagined futures and visitors to talk about fears of their own time.
summary: 1950s science fiction carried atomic-age fears: a visitor warns Earth about its bombs, bomb tests breed giant ants, and pod people have been read as Cold War allegory.

cards.headline: In 1951, a flying saucer landed in Washington with a warning.
cards.body: In The Day the Earth Stood Still, directed by Robert Wise, a visitor named Klaatu arrives and warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations. Britannica calls it a classic that reflects the fears of the Cold War and the early atomic age. The spaceship was imaginary. The worry was not.

cards.headline: Giant ants from a real test site
cards.body: Level 7's A Trip to the Moon was fantasy made with camera tricks such as stop motion and superimposition. By the 1950s, science fiction's monsters had a return address. In Them! (1954), giant ants mutated by atomic bomb tests in the New Mexico desert threaten humanity. Britannica calls it arguably the best of the decade's giant atomic-mutant creature movies. The fear was real; the film just gave it six legs.

cards.headline: Your neighbor, but not quite
cards.body: In Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), directed by Don Siegel, aliens grow in seedpods and take over people's bodies while they sleep, leaving copies with no human emotion. Made at the height of the Cold War, it has been read as a picture of Cold War paranoia, fear of McCarthyism, the alienation of mass society, or life under communism. Siegel said he intended no political message. Each audience found its own fear in the pods.

title: Suspense and Surprise
objective: After this level you can explain Alfred Hitchcock's difference between surprise and suspense, and why giving the audience information builds tension.
summary: Hitchcock's bomb under the table: hide it and you get 15 seconds of surprise; show it and you get 15 minutes of suspense, because the audience takes part. Double Indemnity uses the same idea.

cards.headline: Two people chat at a table. Underneath it, there's a bomb.
cards.body: In 1962 the French director François Truffaut sat down with Alfred Hitchcock for a long series of interviews; the book came out in 1966. To explain the difference between surprise and suspense, Hitchcock described a scene. Same table, same chat, same bomb. Only one thing changes: what you know.

cards.headline: Version one: surprise
cards.body: Two people talk about nothing much. Then, boom. The audience jumps, but everything before the blast was an ordinary scene with nothing at stake as far as anyone could tell. Hitchcock's verdict: you've given the audience 15 seconds of surprise, at the moment of the explosion, and that's all.

mascot.line: Keep this: surprise hides information from you; suspense hands it over. Hitchcock chose to tell.

cards.headline: Version two: suspense
cards.body: Now show the audience the bomb being planted. Let them know it will go off at one o'clock, and put a clock in the scene reading a quarter to one. The same harmless chat becomes fascinating, Hitchcock said, because the audience is now participating in the scene. You want to shout at the screen. That's 15 minutes of suspense instead of 15 seconds of surprise.

cards.headline: Telling you whodunit, on purpose
cards.body: The same logic can run a whole film. Double Indemnity, one of Level 56's noirs, lets you know who committed the crime from the start. Britannica says that makes it a character-driven drama rather than a mystery. You aren't guessing who did it. You're watching what happens to them, and knowing is exactly what keeps you tense.

title: When Genres Bend
objective: After this level you can explain how parodies and revisionist films bend a genre's rules, and why that only works once the rules are familiar.
summary: Parodies like Blazing Saddles and Young Frankenstein (1974) play a genre's rules for laughs; revisionist films like Unforgiven (1992) turn them serious. Both need viewers who know the rules.

cards.headline: A joke about a genre only lands if you know the genre.
cards.body: Britannica points out that often the most acclaimed films invoke a genre's conventions only to break them down. Breaking a rule is only interesting when everyone knows the rule. After decades of Westerns and monster movies, filmmakers had plenty of rules to bend.

cards.headline: Parody: the rules, played for laughs
cards.body: In 1974 Mel Brooks released two parodies. Blazing Saddles spoofs the Western with a Black sheriff at its center, satirizing both racial prejudice and the genre's conventions. Young Frankenstein parodies Universal's Frankenstein films, down to black-and-white photography that copies the look of Bride of Frankenstein (1935). The gags need the old films. You laugh because you recognize what's being bent.

cards.headline: Revision: the rules, turned serious
cards.body: Classic Westerns settle conflicts with violence and physical courage. Revisionist films question that. Britannica traces the Western from Stagecoach to Unforgiven (1992), which it calls an ironic perversion of the genre's codes. Clint Eastwood's film takes an unsentimental look at frontier violence, and it won Academy Awards for best picture and best director. The gunfight is still there. It just stops being fun.

cards.headline: Why familiar has to come first
cards.body: Both moves run on Level 51's genre promise. Viewers know what to expect from a genre film, down to its music, lighting and plot devices, because they've watched so many. Parody plays with that knowledge for laughs; revision turns it against you. Without the rules already in your head, a spoof is just a strange film.

title: Checkpoint: Genres and Why They Work
objective: After this level you can explain why genres work and how filmmakers keep familiar formulas fresh.
summary: Genres can be defined by setting, by story shape or by style: noir may be a style, not a genre. The chapter showed genres as promises, kept fresh by new ideas, suspense and bending the rules.

cards.headline: Is film noir even a genre? Critics still argue.
cards.body: This chapter treated genres as promises. So where does one genre stop and the next begin? Britannica defines film noir as a style of filmmaking, and critics still argue over whether it is a genre at all. That argument turns out to be a neat way to sum up the chapter.

cards.headline: A place, a shape or a look
cards.body: Most genres are defined by subject or setting: the Western, the gangster film, science fiction. The musical is looser. It often has a show-business setting, but it can be about almost any subject. Film noir is looser still: the label fits mostly crime dramas, yet some critics apply it to certain Westerns and comedies, and there's a running debate over whether it's a genre at all or a style shared by many.

Screwball couples fought their way to love, since sparring stood in for what the code banned. Horror aimed for just-right fear. Noir and science fiction carried the worries of their time. Hitchcock showed that letting the audience in on a secret builds suspense. And once the rules were familiar, filmmakers could bend them.

title: Italian Neorealism
objective: After this level you can explain why postwar Italian filmmakers shot real streets with nonprofessional actors, as in Bicycle Thieves.
summary: After Fascism fell, Italian Neorealism took cameras into Rome's war-damaged streets. De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948) cast non-professionals in a small story of a stolen bicycle.

cards.headline: In 1948, a whole film hung on one stolen bicycle.
cards.body: A poor man in postwar Rome finally gets a job pasting up posters, and the job needs a bicycle. Then someone steals it. Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves follows him and his young son across the city, searching. No stars, no studio sets. Why would filmmakers choose to work like that?

cards.headline: Cinema out of the rubble
cards.body: Italian Neorealism had roots in the 1920s, but Fascist control held it back for nearly two decades. When the Fascist regime fell at the end of World War II, it burst out. Roberto Rossellini shot Open City (1945) just months after the Allies freed Rome, on the city's rubble-strewn streets, with a cast that included many non-actors. The BFI notes it was made with scraps of film stock. The war had wrecked the city, so the city became the set.

cards.headline: Real streets, real faces
cards.body: Neorealist films aimed for a documentary-like objectivity: their actors were, or looked like, ordinary people in everyday situations. Bicycle Thieves was shot on location in Rome, and its father and son were played by non-professionals, Lamberto Maggiorani and Enzo Staiola. De Sica was drawn to Maggiorani's callused worker's hands and the way he moved. You can't get that from a costume department.

cards.headline: A small story on purpose
cards.body: The plot is tiny. Antonio's new job is pasting posters on walls, and it requires a bicycle, so a stolen bike puts the job itself at risk. That is the whole engine of the film. Neorealism found its drama in commonplace situations like this one: no villain's lair, no grand rescue, just a father, a son and a missing bicycle.

title: The French New Wave
objective: After this level you can explain how young French critics turned directors in the late 1950s broke Hollywood's rules with cheap, loose filmmaking.
summary: In the late 1950s, critics from Cahiers du cinéma such as Truffaut and Godard began directing. Low budgets, handheld cameras and visible jump cuts became the New Wave's style.

cards.headline: What happens when the film critics grab the cameras?
cards.body: In the 1950s, a group of young French critics wrote sharp reviews of what was wrong with French films. By the late 1950s, several of them, including François Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard, were making their own. Their films looked cheap, loose and fast. What rules were they breaking, and why did it work?

cards.headline: From the review page to the director's chair
cards.body: Truffaut and Godard came out of the film magazine Cahiers du cinéma. For eight years there, Truffaut was the harshest critic of French films, which he found stale and conventional. The New Wave pushed back against the well-built plot, the merely craftsmanlike approach and the polished 'tradition of quality'. Then, in 1959, Truffaut's semiautobiographical The 400 Blows won the best direction prize at Cannes. The critic had become the one to beat.

cards.headline: Breathless, on a shoestring
cards.body: Godard's Breathless (1960) was made with low-budget, guerrilla methods. Cinematographer Raoul Coutard shot it handheld. When a scene called for a smooth tracking shot and the production couldn't afford tracks, Coutard sat in a wheelchair and was pushed along. Making do became part of the look.

mascot.line: Keep this: the New Wave's rough edges started as budget fixes, then became a style chosen on purpose.

cards.headline: Cuts you can see
cards.body: Breathless ran long. Instead of removing whole scenes, Godard cut inside them, leaving little jumps in time where the trims were. These jump cuts break continuity and remind you that you're watching a film. The New Wave also proved something to the business: a film could be a commercial and an artistic success at once.

title: Kurosawa and Rashomon
objective: After this level you can explain how Rashomon told one event from clashing points of view and why its 1951 prize opened the West to Japanese film.
summary: Kurosawa's Rashomon (1950) shows one crime recalled differently by four people. Its 1951 Golden Lion at Venice brought Japanese film serious attention worldwide.

cards.headline: Four witnesses. One crime. Four different stories.
cards.body: In Kurosawa Akira's Rashomon (1950), a samurai is murdered and his wife is attacked. Four people each tell what happened, and their versions don't match. Which one do you believe?

cards.headline: One event, four versions
cards.body: Kurosawa built the film from two short stories by Ryunosuke Akutagawa. The samurai, his wife, a bandit and a woodcutter each recall the same crime in a distinctly different way, and the film lets you see each version. Usually the camera is the most trustworthy witness in the room. Here it shows you four pasts that can't all be true.

cards.headline: A film about truth itself
cards.body: Showing one event through different people's eyes caught audiences' imagination. It pushed the idea that cinema could probe a deep philosophical problem, and Britannica calls Rashomon a meditation on the nature of truth. The question stops being who did it, and becomes whether anyone can tell it straight.

cards.headline: A prize that opened a door
cards.body: In 1951, Rashomon won the Golden Lion, the top prize at the Venice Film Festival. It was the first time a Japanese film had won such high international acclaim. Afterward, Japanese films drew serious attention around the world, and new export markets opened in the West. One prize, and a whole national cinema got an audience.

title: Ozu's Quiet Style
objective: After this level you can explain how Yasujirō Ozu's low, still camera and simple cuts turned family life into drama.
summary: Yasujirō Ozu filmed family life from a low, still camera, avoided fades and dissolves, and set pillow shots between scenes, as in Tokyo Story (1953).

cards.headline: A camera that sits on the floor and barely moves.
cards.body: Many directors move the camera to make a scene exciting. Yasujirō Ozu did nearly the opposite: he set it low, gave up almost all camera movement and let a family's ordinary days play out. How can a camera that stays so still make audiences feel so much?

cards.headline: Drama about ordinary families
cards.body: Ozu was a leading director of the shomin-geki, 'common-people's drama', about lower-middle-class Japanese family life. In Tokyo Story (1953), an aged couple leave their seaside hometown of Onomichi for their first trip to Tokyo, to visit the families of their two eldest children. No chases, no crimes. The biggest event is a family visit, and that is plenty.

mascot.line: Keep this: low, still, no fades. Ozu stripped the style down so the family could fill the frame.

cards.headline: Low, still and straight
cards.body: Ozu framed his scenes from a low angle, as if seated on a tatami mat, and stuck to a single 50mm lens. He almost totally gave up camera movement for straight, still shots. In Tokyo Story, fades and dissolves are nowhere to be seen, and tracking shots are rare. With so little moving, the small things people do take center stage.

cards.headline: A breath between scenes
cards.body: Between scenes, Ozu often cut to short, still views of the world: seas and mountains, boats, train tracks, buildings and rooms. Critic Noël Burch named them 'pillow shots', after the pillow words of classical poetry. They keep the film's gentle, measured rhythm, like a pause before the next line.

title: Satyajit Ray
objective: After this level you can explain how Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali brought a realist style to Indian cinema.
summary: Inspired by Bicycle Thieves, Satyajit Ray made Pather Panchali (1955) on location against the odds; its naturalistic portrait of a poor Bengal village family won at Cannes in 1956.

cards.headline: Two children run through a field to see a train go by.
cards.body: In Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali (1955), young Apu and his sister race through a paddy field to glimpse a passing train. It's one of the film's most memorable scenes, and it was made by a director who had never made a film before. How did he pull it off?

cards.headline: A book designer sees Bicycle Thieves
cards.body: Ray started in advertising as an art director and became a leading Indian typographer and book-jacket designer. He had illustrated an edition of Bibhutibhushan Banerjee's novel Pather Panchali and began to imagine it on screen. De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (Level 61) showed him a film could be shot on location with non-professional actors, and meeting director Jean Renoir in Bengal in 1949 spurred him on.

cards.headline: Made against the odds
cards.body: Bengali producers distrusted his unconventional approach, so Ray began shooting in late 1952 with his own money and an inexperienced crew. The West Bengal government eventually helped, reluctantly. The film took two and a half years to finish. Not a quick start for a career.

cards.headline: Ordinary life, Bengal style
cards.body: The BFI calls Pather Panchali a naturalistic portrait of ordinary lives: a poor rural family in Bengal, with all its mischief, discoveries, joys and tragedies. It succeeded with critics and at the box office, and won a major award at the 1956 Cannes festival. That success let Ray make the rest of his Apu trilogy.

title: Songs in Indian Popular Cinema
objective: After this level you can explain why popular Hindi films weave song and dance into their stories and use playback singers.
summary: India's first talkie, Alam Ara (1931), was full of songs. Popular Hindi films inherited song from Parsi theatre, use it in every genre, and rely on playback singers.

cards.headline: In 1931, India's first talking picture was also a singing one.
cards.body: Alam Ara, India's first talkie, was advertised as 'All talking, all singing, all dancing' and packed in seven song sequences. Songs are still at the heart of popular Hindi films, whatever their genre. Why do these stories stop for a song, and who is really singing?

cards.headline: The songs came before the cinema
cards.body: Hindi film didn't invent the song-filled story. Parsi theatre, which flourished from the 1850s to the 1930s, combined folk and musical theatre traditions and was a forerunner of Bollywood, the Hindi film industry named from Bombay plus Hollywood. When sound reached Indian cinema in 1931, the screen could finally sing too.

cards.headline: Not a genre, an ingredient
cards.body: In Hollywood, the musical is one genre among many. In Bollywood, song and dance turn up in all the others, from family dramas to action films. They're good business, too: Britannica notes that soundtracks and choreographed set pieces are often the engines that drive a film's box office. A hit song sells the ticket.

cards.headline: The voice behind the star
cards.body: Here's the twist: the star on screen usually isn't the one singing. Playback singers prerecord the songs, and the actors lip-sync to them; the singers never appear. The greatest became legends anyway. Lata Mangeshkar recorded songs for more than 2,000 Indian films. One voice, many faces.

title: Hong Kong Action
objective: After this level you can explain how Hong Kong studios turned martial arts and stunt choreography into a style copied around the world.
summary: Bruce Lee's realistic kung fu made Hong Kong action famous; Jackie Chan and Yuen Woo-ping, trained in Peking opera, added comedy, real stunts and wirework that Hollywood adopted.

cards.headline: Hollywood's action heroes learned some of their best moves from Hong Kong.
cards.body: When The Matrix (1999) needed its fights, the work went to Hong Kong choreographer Yuen Woo-ping, and Hollywood action changed. How did one city's studios teach the world to fight on film?

cards.headline: Bruce Lee makes it real
cards.body: Bruce Lee's first Hong Kong films, The Big Boss (1971) and Fist of Fury (1972), were huge hits. The speed of his punches and the fluidity of his kicks, built on rigorous training, gave them a fresh feeling of realism. Then came Enter the Dragon (1973), the first joint venture between Hong Kong and U.S. production companies, and a worldwide hit. Lee died on July 20, 1973, before it was released.

cards.headline: Trained on the opera stage
cards.body: Two of the biggest names learned their moves in opera. From age 7 to 17, Jackie Chan studied acrobatics, singing, martial arts and mime at a strict Peking opera school. Yuen Woo-ping was born into a family of Peking Opera performers, a tradition where drama, martial arts, acrobatics and dance were inseparable. To them, a fight was a kind of dance.

cards.headline: Comedy, stunts and wires
cards.body: In 1978, Yuen's first two films as director, Snake in the Eagle's Shadow and Drunken Master, gave Chan his signature bumbling physical comedy. Chan became famous for doing his own dangerous stunts; a fall in 1986 fractured his skull. And Yuen's Hong Kong wirework, harnesses and cables that lift performers through the air, reshaped Hollywood action with The Matrix.

title: Nollywood
objective: After this level you can explain how Nigeria's film industry grew from cheap video films sold on cassettes in the 1990s.
summary: When the naira's fall ended celluloid filmmaking in Nigeria, Living in Bondage (1992) went straight to VHS and sparked a fast, low-budget video industry later called Nollywood.

cards.headline: A film industry built on videocassettes.
cards.body: In 1992, a Nigerian film called Living in Bondage skipped cinema screens. It went straight to VHS tape and became a smash hit. Why would a country's movies grow up on cassettes?

cards.headline: When celluloid slipped out of reach
cards.body: In the 1980s, Nigeria's currency, the naira, was devalued. Film equipment became hard to come by, and movie theaters grew harder and harder to reach. By the early 1990s, making films on celluloid had stopped altogether. If stories were going to reach people, they needed another road.

cards.headline: Straight to tape
cards.body: Living in Bondage took that road. Britannica dates Nigeria's video film industry to its 1992 release: sold straight to VHS, it became a hit and revolutionized Nigerian cinema. Others followed fast, on small budgets, most shot in about a week. The industry makes films in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and other Nigerian languages.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the order: celluloid got out of reach, video stepped in, the name came last.

title: Film Festivals
objective: After this level you can explain what festivals like Venice and Cannes do and how they carry films from one country to the world.
summary: Venice (1932) is the oldest film festival; Cannes, planned for 1939, opened in 1946. Their prizes and markets carry films across borders.

cards.headline: A film from Japan wins in Italy, and the world starts watching.
cards.body: Remember Rashomon (Level 63)? Its Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 opened Western markets to Japanese films. That's a festival's superpower: one screening can carry a film across borders. How do festivals pull it off?

cards.headline: The oldest and its rival
cards.body: The Venice Film Festival, founded in 1932 as part of the Venice Biennale, is the world's oldest film festival; its top prize is the Golden Lion. France's Philippe Erlanger imagined a rival, a festival free of political pressure. Cannes was due to open on 1 September 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland. It finally opened in 1946.

title: From Radio to Television
objective: After this level you can explain how American television borrowed its networks, shows and advertisers from radio.
summary: American TV borrowed radio's networks: NBC, CBS and ABC began in radio. Radio's stars, led by Milton Berle and CBS's 1948 talent raid, and its advertisers came along.

cards.headline: Early TV was called 'radio with pictures.'
cards.body: Television was first regarded by many as radio with pictures. In 1948 TV was still in its experimental stage, and radio remained the number one broadcast medium. So when television grew up, where did it get its networks, its stars and its money? From the medium it was about to overtake.

cards.headline: The networks came first
cards.body: NBC was formed in 1926. On November 15 that year, 25 radio stations in 21 cities carried its first network program from New York. Later the FCC refused licenses to companies running more than one network, so NBC had to sell its Blue radio network, which became ABC. Meanwhile NBC opened its first TV station in 1939, and by 1948 its TV network had 47 stations. TV's big networks were radio networks with cameras added.

cards.headline: Mr. Television
cards.body: Radio's biggest stars, such as Jack Benny, Bob Hope, and George Burns and Gracie Allen, were at first reluctant to risk their careers on TV. Milton Berle, who had had little success on radio, jumped in. His Texaco Star Theatre on NBC, from 1948, was TV's first hit and set off a dramatic rise in TV set sales. When it debuted, fewer than 2 percent of US homes had a set; by 1956, 70 percent did.

cards.headline: The talent raid
cards.body: CBS also began as a radio network, in the late 1920s, and grew under William S. Paley. In 1948 Paley signed radio stars away from NBC, including Jack Benny and George Burns and Gracie Allen. They proved as popular on TV as they had been on radio. The fight for television's future started as a fight over radio's stars.

cards.headline: Who paid for it all
cards.body: Advertising became the main way American broadcasting paid its bills: sponsored network programs brought money to both the network and its stations. Sponsors had a say, too. On NBC radio, breakout hits on the Blue network were often moved to the more popular Red network at sponsors' request. Television inherited the whole deal.

title: The Network Era
objective: After this level you can explain how three national networks shaped what nearly all Americans watched from the 1950s to the 1970s.
summary: Four networks began regular schedules in 1948; DuMont folded, and ABC, CBS and NBC shaped what nearly everyone watched. By the late 1970s they held over 90 percent of prime time.

cards.headline: Three channels, nearly everybody watching
cards.body: In the late 1970s, more than 90 percent of the US prime-time audience was watching ABC, CBS or NBC. Three companies, one country's evenings. How did television end up with so few doors to walk through?

cards.headline: Four networks, then three
cards.body: Regular programming on the four networks, ABC, CBS, NBC and DuMont, was scarce until the fall of 1948. DuMont folded in the mid-1950s, leaving three. Their battleground was prime time, the evening block from 8 to 11 PM Eastern. Three networks splitting three hours a night: that was the whole menu.

cards.headline: One night, 70 million viewers
cards.body: By 1960 nearly 90 percent of American homes had a television. On September 26 that year, the first televised presidential debate, between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon, was carried on all three networks at once and reached a then-record audience of about 70 million. With every channel showing the same event, the country watched together.

cards.headline: Cultural glue
cards.body: Britannica calls broadcasting a kind of cultural glue: from 1929 to 1989, nearly the whole country, young and old, rich and poor, fed from the same cultural trough. Control of television by three companies produced a unified mass culture that nearly everyone experienced. Three choices meant one shared screen.

title: Live TV's Golden Age
objective: After this level you can explain why early TV drama was performed live and what changed when shows moved to film and videotape.
summary: Early network TV was mostly live, and anthology series staged new plays weekly. Kinescopes filmed a monitor to record shows; Ampex videotape (1956) and filmed Hollywood series ended the live era.

cards.headline: In the early 1950s, most TV went out live.
cards.body: In the early 1950s most network television was broadcast live: whatever happened in the studio happened in your living room. By the early 1960s most of it was recorded. What was live TV like, and what ended it?

cards.headline: A new play every week
cards.body: Most TV plays of the era were anthology dramas: weekly series presenting a different play under one title, such as Kraft Television Theatre (1947 to 1958) and Studio One (1948 to 1958). Young writers such as Paddy Chayefsky, Rod Serling and Gore Vidal made their names there. Chayefsky's Marty began as a 1953 television play and became a 1955 film that won the Academy Award for best picture.

cards.headline: Filming a TV screen
cards.body: Before videotape, the only way to record TV was on film. A movie camera pointed at a TV monitor made a kinescope, which was developed and later projected for broadcast in other time zones. The picture was poor, and the film could be used only once. By 1954, TV broadcasters were using more raw film than the entire movie industry.

cards.headline: Tape, and a move to Hollywood
cards.body: In 1956 Ampex introduced the first practical videotape recorder for TV stations. On November 30, 1956, CBS taped a live New York newscast in Hollywood and rebroadcast it hours later to the West Coast. Production moved to the Los Angeles area, and the live style gave way to shows recorded on film, which could earn money indefinitely from reruns. Recorded TV could pay again and again.

title: The Sitcom
objective: After this level you can explain how the situation comedy works and how I Love Lucy's filmed, three-camera method made reruns possible.
summary: A sitcom is a half-hour show with a continuing cast in one setting. I Love Lucy, filmed in Hollywood with three cameras before a live audience, set the standard and became an early rerun.

cards.headline: I Love Lucy was shot on film while most TV went out live.
cards.body: I Love Lucy, starring Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz, debuted on CBS in October 1951. Most shows were then made in the East, broadcast live there and shown to western time zones as kinescopes, which a Library of Congress specialist likened to watching TV through a cheesecloth. Ball and Arnaz chose to make theirs in Hollywood, on film. Why did that choice matter?

cards.headline: Same people, same place, every week
cards.body: The sitcom was a 30-minute format with a continuing cast of characters in the same setting week after week. I Love Lucy was adapted from My Favorite Husband, a CBS radio comedy Ball had starred in since 1948. Its early episodes took place mostly in a New York apartment building, where Lucy and Ricky Ricardo lived near their landlords and friends, Fred and Ethel Mertz. You always knew where you were; the fun was what went wrong there.

cards.headline: Three cameras and an audience
cards.body: Cinematographer Karl Freund and director Marc Daniels are generally credited with filming the show with three cameras in front of a live audience, the technique that became the sitcom standard. It was shot on 35 mm film with one lighting system for the whole set. With three cameras rolling, an episode could be filmed straight through, in sequence, like a stage play.

mascot.line: Keep this: shooting on film is what let Lucy air again and again. Every rerun you've seen owes something to that choice.

cards.headline: Cut it, then show it again
cards.body: Three cameras meant three streams of film. Editor Dann Cahn cut the show on a Moviola with four heads: three for picture and one for sound. And because it was made on film, I Love Lucy could be shown again: in 1955 it became one of the first series broadcast as reruns.

cards.headline: Cronkite's half hour

cards.headline: The war in the living room

In their living rooms, Americans regularly saw film of airplanes flying, often dropping bombs, and troops on patrol, sometimes in combat. The footage wasn't instant: it usually reached the networks as cans of film shipped by air, arriving a few days later.

cards.headline: The anchor goes to look

title: Ads and Ratings
objective: After this level you can explain how advertising paid for broadcast TV and how ratings measured audiences to set its price.
summary: After the rigged quiz shows of the late 1950s, networks stopped selling whole shows to single sponsors and sold short commercials. Nielsen ratings measured audiences and set the price.

cards.headline: Broadcast TV was free to watch. Somebody still had to pay.
cards.body: Advertising was the main support of American broadcasting, and networks used ratings, in part, to set the advertising price of each program. So two questions ran the business: who controlled the shows, and how many people were watching?

cards.headline: The quiz shows were fixed
cards.body: In 1958 former contestants revealed that big-money TV quiz shows were rigged and contestants coached, and a House subcommittee held hearings in 1959. Afterward, networks grew wary of single-sponsor programs and sold time in 15-, 30- and 60-second units. Producers took control of shows, and time was sold the way magazines sell ad pages. With advertisers out of the shows, their urge to interfere faded.

cards.headline: A box on the TV set
cards.body: From 1950, A.C. Nielsen rated TV shows using a sample of more than 1,000 TV homes. Each had a small box, the Audimeter, attached to the set to record when it was on and what channel it was tuned to, and a smaller group kept viewing diaries. A thousand homes stood in for a whole country's living rooms.

cards.headline: Rating versus share
cards.body: A rating of 20 means 20 percent of all US TV households tuned in to a program. A 30 share means 30 percent of the people watching TV at that moment chose it. Networks use ratings to set advertising rates for each program and to decide which programs to keep or cancel. A low number could end a show.

The Carnegie Commission on educational television proposed a law, and on November 7, 1967, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Public Broadcasting Act, creating the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. title: Cable Changes TV
objective: After this level you can explain how cable and satellite channels ended the network era by serving smaller, targeted audiences.
summary: Cable began in the late 1940s to fix poor reception. HBO went national by satellite in 1975 and CNN began in 1980. As cable spread, targeted channels split viewers and the network era ended.

cards.headline: Cable TV began as a fix for bad reception.
cards.body: US cable systems began in the late 1940s to improve reception of network broadcasts in remote and hilly areas. A wire brought in the signal the hills blocked. Some systems went on to deliver 50 or more channels. What happens to three networks when viewers have fifty doors?

cards.headline: Movies, news and a satellite
cards.body: HBO started in 1972 showing uncut, commercial-free movies, and subscribers paid extra for it. In 1975 it became the first American network to deliver its programming by satellite, which made it the first national cable channel. CNN began in 1980 and ushered in the era of 24-hour news. Cable wasn't a repair job anymore; it was programming.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the percentages. Remember the direction: cable went up, and the big three's share came down.

cards.headline: Smaller audiences, many screens

title: Streaming and the Binge
objective: After this level you can explain how streaming changed when, where and how people watch, and how series were written for binge viewing.
summary: Netflix went from DVDs by mail (1997) to streaming (2007) to whole seasons at once (2013). Autoplay made binge-watching easy, and writers began shaping seasons like one long film.

cards.headline: In 2013, a whole season arrived on the same day.
cards.body: In February 2013 Netflix made all 13 first-season episodes of House of Cards available at once, instead of one a week. You no longer waited for the network's schedule. How did watching get here, and what did it do to the shows themselves?

cards.headline: From the mailbox to the stream
cards.body: Netflix was founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph as a DVD-rental service: subscribers ordered online and received discs by mail. In 2007 it introduced streaming, letting subscribers watch directly over the Internet. Viewers quickly embraced having all of a new season to watch at their own pace, on whatever screen they wished. The schedule moved from the network to you.

cards.headline: Bingeing is older than streaming
cards.body: To binge-watch is to watch many or all episodes of a series in rapid succession. It predates Netflix: cable networks aired marathons of classic shows in the late 1990s, and binging became routine with TV on DVD a decade later. Streaming made it effortless: on Netflix, the next episode queues up as soon as the last one ends.

cards.headline: Writing a 10-hour movie
cards.body: Broadcast writers build peril at the end of each act to keep you watching through the commercial break. Binge viewers don't need that pull, and they skip the 'previously on' recap. Writer Marc Bernardin notes that writers now describe planning a streaming season as 'breaking a 10-hour movie'. How you watch changed what gets written.

title: New Hollywood
objective: After this level you can explain how a new generation of directors took creative control in Hollywood between the late 1960s and 1980, and what they borrowed from the New Wave.
summary: Surprise hits, TV and foreign films opened Hollywood to young directors from the late 1960s. Bonnie and Clyde borrowed from the New Wave; blockbusters and Heaven's Gate ended the era.

cards.headline: In 1967, two movie bank robbers helped hand Hollywood to its directors.
cards.body: Bonnie and Clyde (1967), The Graduate (1967) and Easy Rider (1969) were surprise hits, and they opened an era now called New Hollywood. For about fifteen years, directors, not studio bosses, seemed to call the shots. How did that happen, and why didn't it last?

cards.headline: The audience was already leaving
cards.body: The old studios had competition on two sides. Audiences were drifting to television, and many were drawn to bold films from abroad: the French New Wave, Italian Neorealism, the work of Kurosawa Akira. New Hollywood, running roughly from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s, answered with what Britannica calls a decisive rejection of the studio system in favor of director-driven creativity and experimentation.

cards.headline: A Hollywood film with a French accent
cards.body: Bonnie and Clyde, directed by Arthur Penn, tore down barriers in how the screen showed violence and sexuality. Its writers, David Newman and Robert Benton, loved Truffaut and Godard. Truffaut was their first choice to direct; he passed, and Godard declined too. The finished film still carried their mark: its famous final sequence was cut with editing techniques inspired by Godard and Truffaut.

cards.headline: Movie brats, then the money men
cards.body: In the early 1970s a younger group nicknamed the movie brats, among them Coppola, Lucas, Scorsese and Spielberg, often arrived through new film schools. Then the tide turned. After Jaws (1975), studios chased blockbusters and steered away from experiments. Michael Cimino's Western Heaven's Gate (1980) went nearly four times over an already huge budget and was a disaster for United Artists. It also ended most studios' interest in reviving the Western.

title: Jaws and the Blockbuster
objective: After this level you can explain how Jaws in 1975 set the summer blockbuster pattern of wide release and heavy TV advertising.
summary: Jaws (June 20, 1975) opened in more than 400 US theaters at once after a week of TV trailers, and became the first summer blockbuster whose marketing set the standard.

cards.headline: Summer used to be where films went to hide.
cards.body: Before Jaws, summer releases were typically lesser films, because audiences tended to stay away from movie theaters in summer. Then, on June 20, 1975, Universal released Steven Spielberg's film of Peter Benchley's 1974 novel about a shark. How did one film make summer the season for blockbusters?

cards.headline: One city at a time
cards.body: The usual path was slow. A film opened first in a major city, then reached other cities and towns over several weeks. Jaws skipped the queue: it opened in more than 400 theaters across the United States on its first weekend. Instead of waiting for a film to come to town, the whole country could see it at once.

cards.headline: Sold on the small screen
cards.body: A film opening everywhere needs everyone to know about it, fast. In the week before release, Jaws was heavily promoted on television with 30-second trailers. The shark reached living rooms before it reached theaters.

cards.headline: The pattern that stuck
cards.body: Jaws is considered the first summer blockbuster, and its marketing tactics became the standard for the ones that followed, changing how Hollywood marketed and distributed films. Studios drew their own lesson: after its massive success, they began prioritizing potential blockbusters and steering away from experimental, director-driven projects.

title: Movies at Home
objective: After this level you can explain how videotape rental changed how films earned money and why the Betamax case of 1984 mattered.
summary: Studios fought the VCR until the Supreme Court's 1984 Betamax ruling allowed time-shifting. Costly tapes made renting the norm, and rentals became a big share of a film's income.

cards.headline: Hollywood's first answer to the VCR was a lawsuit.
cards.body: Movie studios at first resisted the home video recorder, just as they had resisted television some three decades earlier. A box that could copy what was on TV looked like a threat. Within a few years, it was paying their bills. What changed?

cards.headline: Universal takes Sony to court
cards.body: Universal City Studios sued Sony, maker of the Betamax. Its argument: Betamax owners recorded Universal's copyrighted TV programs, so Sony was liable for their infringement. On January 17, 1984, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4, in an opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens, that selling VCRs to the public was not contributory infringement.

mascot.line: Keep this: a machine with lots of legal uses can be sold, even if some people misuse it.

cards.headline: Time-shifting
cards.body: The key idea was time-shifting: recording a broadcast to watch later at home. The Court held it was fair use. It also held that copying equipment may be sold if it is capable of substantial noninfringing uses. Some owners might misuse a VCR, but plenty of its uses were legal.

cards.headline: Rent, don't buy
cards.body: Early 1980s tapes often cost $100 or more, so most people paid around five dollars to rent one for a night or a few days. By 1983 most studios sold tapes to rental stores and home users. Rentals soon made up a significant share of a film's total revenue, and Hollywood began planning for that income when setting budgets. The machine they fought became part of the paycheck.

title: Independent Film

summary: Independent films are made outside the major studios. Cassavetes's Shadows and Romero's Night of the Living Dead found new ways on little money; Sundance gave independents a stage.

cards.headline: An early American independent film was paid for partly by radio listeners.
cards.body: John Cassavetes financed his first film as director, Shadows, partly with donations sent after he appealed for money on a radio program. No studio, no studio money. What makes a film independent, and what can a tiny budget push a filmmaker to try?

cards.headline: Outside the studio system
cards.body: Independent film simply means films produced outside the major studio system. Shadows shows what that looked like: shot on 16-mm film over about two and a half years, and semi-improvised. It is generally acknowledged to have started the American independent movement. Cassavetes paid for later films with his acting, which was wanted by the same studios that were reluctant to back his directing.

cards.headline: Friends, pooled money, new monsters

It also set the pattern for modern zombie movies by separating the monsters from Vodou and putting them in contemporary settings. A small budget didn't stop a new idea from taking over a genre.

cards.headline: A stage for independents
cards.body: Independents still needed an audience. The Sundance Film Festival began in 1978 in Salt Lake City as the Utah/United States Film Festival. It came under Robert Redford's Sundance Institute, founded to nurture independent filmmakers, and took the Sundance name in 1991. It became known for jump-starting careers, including those of the Coen brothers, Steven Soderbergh and Quentin Tarantino.

title: Miniatures and Matte Paintings
objective: After this level you can explain how models, forced perspective and painted backgrounds created impossible places before computers.
summary: Before computers, cheap scale models, forced perspective, high-speed filming and matte paintings on glass (from Norman Dawn in 1907) put impossible places on screen.

cards.headline: The Emerald City was never built. It was painted.
cards.body: The distant Emerald City in The Wizard of Oz (1939) is a matte painting, and Gone With the Wind is filled with matte-painted backdrops. Before computers, how did filmmakers put places that didn't exist on screen?

cards.headline: Small, cheap and close to the lens
cards.body: One answer was to build small. Miniatures, or scale models, are often used because they are relatively inexpensive and easy to handle. Where you put them matters. Forced perspective makes objects look larger, smaller, nearer or farther than they are, because the closer something is to the camera, the larger it appears. A model near the lens can pass for a building far away.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: filming faster gives slower action on screen, because playback stays at normal speed.

cards.headline: Film it fast to make it big
cards.body: Models can also be filmed at more than 24 frames per second. Played back at normal speed, the action runs in slow motion, which gives a more realistic-looking perspective and time scale. Slow the action down, and a model moves more like the full-size thing.

cards.headline: Painting on glass
cards.body: The other answer was paint. Matte painting is credited to filmmaker Norman Dawn, who first used it in his 1907 film Missions of California. Painters put scenery on a sheet of glass and left parts unpainted. With the glass in front of the camera, the actors were filmed through the clear parts, so they seemed to stand inside the painted world.

title: Stop Motion
objective: After this level you can explain how stop-motion animators move a model a tiny step for every frame, from King Kong in 1933 onward.
summary: Stop motion photographs a model in slightly different positions, frame by frame. Willis O'Brien made King Kong (1933) a star, and inspired Ray Harryhausen.

cards.headline: King Kong was mostly an 18-inch puppet.
cards.body: Britannica calls King Kong (1933) the first significant feature film to star an animated character. Kong himself was mainly an 18-inch (45-cm) puppet. How do you turn a puppet you could hold into a giant on the big screen?

cards.headline: One pose per frame
cards.body: Stop-motion animation photographs objects in slightly different positions to create the illusion of movement. Move the model a hair, take one frame, move it again. If the model moves for every frame, one second of film at the standard 24 frames per second takes 24 separate poses. Patience is the main special effect.

cards.headline: Willis O'Brien's toolkit
cards.body: King Kong, directed by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, featured pioneering effects by Willis O'Brien. Besides the puppet, giant arms, hands and feet were built for close-ups. O'Brien combined his animated models with live action using miniature rear projection and traveling mattes, which join a separately filmed foreground and background into one picture.

cards.headline: From a garage to an army of skeletons
cards.body: After seeing King Kong, Ray Harryhausen began making stop-motion films in his parents' garage, and he later worked with O'Brien. For Jason and the Argonauts (1963), Harryhausen spent four months animating a battle between Jason, two Argonauts and an army of skeletons. One scene, one pose at a time.

title: Hand-Drawn Animation
objective: After this level you can explain how cel animation works and why Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs in 1937 was a gamble.
summary: Cel animation lays clear, painted sheets over a painted background, so only moving parts are redrawn. Snow White (1937), the first US feature-length cartoon, was a costly gamble.

cards.headline: People called it Disney's Folly.
cards.body: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was Walt Disney's biggest gamble to date: an expensive production, worked on by hundreds of technicians, that became known as Disney's Folly. To see why it was such a risk, start with how a hand-drawn cartoon is built.

cards.headline: A drawing on a clear sheet
cards.body: An animation cel is a line drawing on the face of a transparent sheet of cellulose acetate, colored with paint on the back. The idea goes back at least to December 19, 1914, when Earl Hurd applied for a patent on using transparent sheets over a background that was photographed through them.

cards.headline: Draw only what moves
cards.body: Here's the saving. Characters on transparent sheets were laid over painted backgrounds, so only the moving parts had to be drawn. The painted cels were registered, one after another, over the background and photographed on an animation camera stand. The forest gets painted once; only the walker is drawn again and again.

cards.headline: The gamble pays
cards.body: That was the heart of the gamble: Snow White was the first full-length animated feature film from an American studio. On release, it was an immediate box-office sensation, and it set the standard for later Disney animated films. The folly became the model.

title: Computers Make Pictures
objective: After this level you can explain how computer-generated imagery builds a scene from models, textures and light, leading to Toy Story in 1995.
summary: Computer animation builds models from polygons, shades them with light, then generates frames. Toy Story (1995) was the first entirely computer-animated feature.

cards.headline: Toy Story needed 800,000 machine hours.
cards.body: Toy Story took 114,240 frames of computer animation and 800,000 machine hours to render. No camera took any of those pictures. What was the computer doing all that time?

cards.headline: Build it from polygons
cards.body: First, the computer needs a shape. Models such as the famous Utah Teapot are built from many small polygons, flat pieces fitted together, and can be shown as a wire-frame image, like a sculpture made of chicken wire. At this stage the object has a form but no surface.

cards.headline: Paint it with light
cards.body: Next comes the look. In Phong shading, each pixel takes into account the surface texture and all the light sources, which gives more realistic results but slower rendering. Ray tracing goes further: it follows imaginary rays of light through the scene using the laws of reflection and refraction, and it is computationally expensive. Realism costs computer time.

cards.headline: Make it move, frame after frame
cards.body: Once a three-dimensional figure is digitized, a computer can generate a sequence of images that move it through space, and it can supply in-between frames. Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter and made by Pixar with Disney, was the first entirely computer-animated feature. At 24 frames per second, its 114,240 frames make 4,760 seconds, about 79 minutes.

title: From Film to Digital
objective: After this level you can weigh what filmmakers gained and lost as digital cameras and projectors replaced film stock.
summary: Digital cameras took over from the 1990s to the mid-2010s: films travel as files and can be restored. But data can vanish, and no digital format yet lasts like film.

cards.headline: Most movies now never touch a strip of film.
cards.body: In 2018 Martin Scorsese wrote that almost all pictures are shot with digital cameras, and even those shot on film are edited, color-timed and finished digitally. What did filmmakers gain in the switch, and what did they risk?

cards.headline: What digital gave
cards.body: Digital cinematography, which records images digitally rather than on film, began to take off in the 1990s and was dominant by the mid-2010s. Films travel differently too: a theater now usually shows a Digital Cinema Package sent over the internet or on a drive plugged into the projector. And digital restoration can repair damaged frames, giving old films whole new lives.

mascot.line: Keep this: digital made films easier to shoot, send and repair. Film is still the safer way to keep them.

cards.headline: What digital can lose
cards.body: Here's the catch. Digital information sometimes simply disappears, which has happened to more than one major studio picture, so files must be migrated to each new format. The Academy's 2007 report The Digital Dilemma found no digital archival master format or process with longevity equal to film. Scorsese calls film, now on a strong Mylar base, still the most reliable way to preserve movies.

cards.headline: And the look
cards.body: The debate isn't only about storage. Many advocates argue that film has far superior visual quality to digital video. So the trade is a real one: convenience and repair on one side, durability and, for some, a look on the other.

title: Reading a Frame
objective: After this level you can analyze a single frame by looking at composition, setting, costume and where the actors stand.
summary: Mise-en-scène is everything put in front of the camera: setting, costume, lighting and where actors stand. Placement and size in the frame show who matters.

cards.headline: Pause any film. How much is one frame telling you?
cards.body: In Citizen Kane, a small boy plays in the snow, far back in the frame, while the adults indoors decide who will raise him. You haven't heard a word yet, and you already know who has the power. That's a frame talking.

cards.headline: Mise-en-scène: everything in front of the camera
cards.body: Critics call it mise-en-scène, French for "putting in the scene". It covers everything placed before the camera: the setting and its props, the costumes, the lighting, and the actors and where they stand. Yale's Film Analysis guide notes that the setting, which it calls décor, can amplify a character's emotion or a film's whole mood. Reading a frame means asking why each of those things is there.

cards.headline: Rooms and clothes do the talking
cards.body: Costume can signify character, advertise fashions, or make clear distinctions between characters: dress two rivals alike or apart, and you've said something before anyone speaks. Rooms speak too. Remember Level 17's Caligari? Its designers built sets with exaggerated dimensions and deformed angles to show a narrator's tortured mind. That's décor amplifying emotion at full volume.

mascot.line: Keep this: size and distance in the frame are rarely neutral. Ask who is big, who is small and who is far away.

cards.headline: Where people stand, and how big they look
cards.body: Shot scale can bring you close to a character or swallow them in their surroundings. Welles used it in Citizen Kane to show power shifting. The boy Kane is a small figure playing in the snow at the back of the shot while, indoors, adults arrange for someone else to raise him. Thanks to deep focus, both he and they stay sharp.

title: Color and Mood
objective: After this level you can explain how a film's color palette and grading steer mood, and spot it in a scene.
summary: Color establishes mood and character, but no color has a fixed meaning. O Brother, Where Art Thou? was recolored by computer, a pioneer of digital grading.

cards.headline: Why does a green Mississippi summer look like an old, faded postcard?
cards.body: The Coen brothers shot O Brother, Where Art Thou? in summer, when everything was green. On screen it's dusty gold. Nobody repainted the fields. Somebody repainted the film.

cards.headline: Color is a mood dial
cards.body: Color does more than make a film look real or glamorous. Filmmakers use it to build visual patterns and to establish character or emotion. In Juliet of the Spirits (1965), Fellini's first color feature, color separates the heroine's everyday bourgeois life from her fantasy daydreams. Change the colors and you change the world she seems to live in.

cards.headline: Red doesn't always mean the same thing
cards.body: It's tempting to keep a dictionary: red equals passion, blue equals sadness. Films don't obey it. Yale's Film Analysis guide contrasts red as unrestrained passion in Zhang Yimou's Ju Dou (1990) with red as stagnation and tainted blood in Ingmar Bergman's Cries and Whispers (1972). Same color, opposite feelings. So read a color in its film, not in a dictionary.

cards.headline: Grading: recoloring after the shoot
cards.body: O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000) was the first live-action film extensively color-corrected, or graded, by computer. The Coens wanted a sepia, old-timey look, but the Mississippi locations were far too green. Cinematographer Roger Deakins spent a reported 11 weeks adjusting the digital image, yellowing it. In Technicolor's day, color was set in the lab with dyes; here it was dialed in on a screen.
